identity.plain_name: The lever catch on toolboxes and cases: hook the loop over a catch on the lid, press the lever down and it pulls the lid tight shut with a snap, and it stays shut until you lift the lever
aliases: case latch / toolbox latch / box latch
latch clamp / latch-action (hook-type) toggle clamp (heavier versions)
adjustable draw latch (with a threaded hook or rod)
flexible draw latch / rubber T-handle latch
wire bail closure (Kilner-type jars and swing-top bottles)
Bügelverschluss (German; also used for swing-top closures)
identity.one_liner: A two-part latch in which a lever on one part carries a loop or hook that catches a keeper on the other part; closing the lever swings the loop's pivot past the line between the lever pivot and the keeper (over centre), pulling the parts tightly together and locking them there until the lever is lifted.
identity.complexity: A few parts: a base plate fixed to one part, a lever (handle) pivoted on the base, a loop, hook or wire bail pivoted part-way along the lever, and a keeper (catch plate or strike) fixed to the other part. Many add a threaded hook or rod for adjustment, a spring, a padlock hole or a secondary safety catch. Flexible versions are just a stretchy rubber T-handle and a keeper.
identity.how_it_works: The loop hangs from a pivot on the lever that is offset from the lever's own pivot. Hook the loop over the keeper and push the lever down: the loop's pivot swings towards, then just past, the straight line joining the lever pivot and the keeper (over centre), pulling the two parts together and stretching the loop and any gasket slightly. Once past centre, the pull between the parts tries to close the lever further, against its stop, so the latch cannot open by itself; lifting the lever back past centre releases it (Wikipedia 'Latch'; US patent 4,925,221; RS). Flexible (rubber) draw latches have no lever: the stretch of an EPDM rubber strap hooked over the keeper provides the pull (Boat Outfitters; HTF Hardware).

job: join and hold: holds a lid, door, hatch or panel shut
lock, and release by hand: opens and closes with one flick of the lever; many take a padlock or have a secondary lock
tighten and hold tension: draws the two parts together and keeps them squeezed, removing rattle
seal it, or pass cables or fluid through: only indirectly, by squeezing a lid onto a gasket or O-ring, which does the actual sealing (Southco)
finder_attributes.motion: rotate: the lever and loop swing on pins through a limited arc (Firgelli gives roughly 90-180 degrees for the lever [uncertain]); the joined parts are pulled together by only a small distance
finder_attributes.degrees_of_freedom: 1 while closing: the lever angle sets the position of the loop and the gap between the parts; effectively 0 once closed and locked over centre
special_behaviour: over-centre (snaps past a point and stays): the loop's pivot passes the line between the lever pivot and the keeper and the latch snaps shut (RS: once past the cam point it 'will snap soundly into place and remain securely closed')
self-locking (holds under load, won't back-drive): pulling the parts apart pushes the lever harder into its closed position
hand-release only (locks under load, releases when a person operates it): only lifting the lever opens it
quick-release: opens and closes by hand with no tools
tensioning (takes up slack and holds): draws the parts together and holds a preload, which compresses gaskets and stops rattles (Southco)
holding_principle: shape (form-fit): the loop or hook physically hooks over the keeper
friction or clamping (force-fit): the over-centre lever holds the two parts pressed together with a preload
spring force (a spring or springy part presses it in place): flexible latches hold by the stretch of rubber, and the steel loops of rigid latches stretch very slightly
finder_attributes.input_output: not applicable: it is a fastening latch, not a drive. For reference, the lever multiplies hand force by roughly the handle length divided by the offset of the loop's pivot (the Firgelli blog's example: a 65 mm handle and 5 mm offset give about 13:1) [uncertain]
finder_attributes.removability: tool-free quick release: it opens and closes by hand; the latch body and keeper are screwed, bolted or riveted on and can be removed with tools
finder_attributes.reuse_cycles: many times: opening and closing is its normal use; metal latches last many thousands of cycles, while rubber straps age and printed plastic latches wear and creep sooner [uncertain]
finder_attributes.tools_needed: None to open or close. To fit: a drill and a screwdriver (screws or bolts) or a rivet tool; a spanner to set a threaded hook; optionally a padlock
finder_attributes.seal: none by itself. It is used to make a seal watertight or dust-resistant by pressing a lid onto a gasket or O-ring (Southco: draw latches give 'mechanical advantage to compress gaskets and ensure sealing'). Maker example: a printed rugged box with a TPU seal and tight printed latches survived 10 minutes under 10 cm of water with no leak (zx82net)
finder_attributes.load: Light to heavy in tension (pulling the two parts together). For example, Southco's A1 adjustable draw latches are rated up to 1,550 N (350 lb), 3,110 N (700 lb) and 4,450 N (1,000 lb) for small, medium and large sizes; RS groups latches into light, medium and heavy duty. Weak sideways (shear) and against prying, so let hinges, lips or locating pins take sideways loads [uncertain]. The keeper and its screws must be as strong as the latch (RS)
finder_attributes.adjustable: Yes on adjustable models: a threaded hook or rod changes the reach and the clamping force (Southco A1: grip range up to 144 mm and span adjustment up to 33 mm). Fixed models are adjusted by moving or shimming the keeper. Printed latches can be tuned by scaling the latch by about 2% in X and Y (zx82net)
finder_attributes.play_and_precision: No play once closed, because it is preloaded. It tolerates small misalignment, but the keeper position matters: set too far away, the lever can't pass centre; set too close, it closes loosely, and an over-adjusted latch can even end up exactly on centre, looking closed but unlocked (US patent 4,925,221). Rubber latches tolerate misalignment best (Boat Outfitters). Wikipedia notes a draw latch does not need to be fully closed to hold the two halves together
finder_attributes.access_needed: one side only (blind): both parts are fixed with screws or rivets from the outside and it is operated from outside; through-bolts need both sides
finder_attributes.materials: Stainless steel (corrosion-resistant, marine and industrial), zinc-plated steel or die-cast zinc (low cost), brass or chrome-plated brass (appearance, light to medium duty), acetal (RS); plastic bodies in polypropylene, nylon or glass-filled nylon, and rubber (Southco); EPDM rubber for flexible latches (HTF Hardware). Printed latches in PETG (preferred outdoors) or PLA, with steel screws or rod as pins
finder_attributes.maker_difficulty: easy: cheap to buy and screw on; printable versions, even print-in-place ones, work well for light boxes and cases

processes: off-the-shelf part: the usual choice; many sizes and materials
3D print (FDM): print-in-place latches, or separate printed parts pinned with M3-M5 screws or steel rod
sheet metal: commercial latches are usually stamped steel parts [uncertain]
making.print_in_place: yes: ConceivablyEngineering's 'Sturdy print-in-place draw latch' prints already assembled with no supports and 0.2-0.3 mm gaps. Stronger printed latches are printed as separate parts joined with bolts or steel rod (TECbot, Glenn Brockett, the parametric Rugged Storage Box).
making.making_tips_3d_printing: 1) Geometry: the loop's pivot must swing past the line from the lever pivot to the keeper, or the latch won't snap closed; mount the hook or keeper so this happens (TECbot: 'make sure the hook is mounted low enough that the loop passes the center pivot'). Add a stop on the lever so it can't over-travel. 2) Print-in-place: 0.2-0.3 mm gaps between moving parts, slight under-extrusion especially on the first layer so the joints free up, thick shells (1.2 mm) with infill of secondary importance; the latch can be fixed with up to four M3 screws or glued (ConceivablyEngineering). 3) Pins: bolts (M5 main pivot in TECbot's latch, with the nut pressed flush using a soldering iron) or steel rod (Glenn Brockett uses 2.2 mm welding rod; filament 'may work, not advised'). The Rugged Storage Box fixes each latch with two M3x40 screws that act as pins. 4) Strength and layers: 'You MUST have good layer adhesion or it will break' (Glenn Brockett). zx82net recommends at least 3 perimeters and over 30% infill for latches and hinges. 5) Material: PETG for outdoor or long-term use; zx82net found PLA latches work at first but can creep over time, loosening the latch and the seal; PLA softens above about 60 °C (Prusa). 6) Tuning: print two sizes and pick the tightness you like; scaling the latch by 2% in X and Y makes a significant difference (zx82net). Tight tolerances may need a little trimming (Glenn Brockett). 7) Sealing: for a watertight box, add a flexible seal (TPU gasket or a 1.75 mm TPU filament in a groove) for the latch to squeeze (zx82net; Rugged Storage Box). 8) Keep printed latches for boxes and light panels; they are 'not sturdy compared to non-printed, non-plastic latches' (ConceivablyEngineering).
making.off_the_shelf_parts: Draw latches / toggle latches in fixed-grip, adjustable (threaded hook or U-bolt) and locking (padlockable or key-locking) versions, with matching keepers (catch plates or strikes); concealed and rotary draw latches; flexible rubber T-handle draw latches with keepers; latch-action toggle clamps (hook or U-bolt with latch plate) for heavy lids and doors; latches with a secondary safety catch; wire bail closures for jars (Southco; RS; Carr Lane; Boat Outfitters).
rules_of_thumb: Choose a latch whose ultimate tensile strength (UTS) is roughly double the force it will see, and make sure the keeper (catch or strike plate) is rated as strongly as the latch (RS).
Longer handles need less force to close against the same over-centre resistance (RS).
The loop must pass the centre pivot for the over-centre action to work (TECbot, Printables 'Over-Center Toggle Latch').

Adjust carefully: under-adjustment leaves a gap that lets vibration and airflow work on the panel; over-adjustment can reduce the over-centre movement or leave the latch looking closed while sitting on centre, unlocked, which is why the aircraft toggle latch in US patent 4,925,221 adds an automatic safety catch.
Printed draw latches: 0.2-0.3 mm print-in-place gaps and 1.2 mm shells (ConceivablyEngineering); scaling by 2% changes tightness noticeably (zx82net).

Blog guidance on spacing and preload: about one latch per 200-300 mm of gasket perimeter with one within 100 mm of each corner; the latch should close about 1-3 mm past dead centre; rubber latches should be stretched to about 110-115% of their free length (Firgelli) [uncertain].

everyday_examples: Flight cases, instrument cases and aluminium transport cases (Wikimedia Commons photo of case latches)
The latch that tightens the ring of a springform cake pan (Wikipedia 'Latch')
The wire clip on Kilner-type jars and swing-top bottles (Rowse; Wikipedia 'Flip-top')
guidance.when_to_use: Use a draw latch when a lid, door or panel must be pulled tightly closed and opened quickly by hand: cases and toolboxes, access panels and machine covers, boxes with a gasket that must be squeezed to keep water or dust out, and anything that rattles. It suits places where the catch is on a separate part from the latch, and where some misalignment must be pulled in. Choose a rubber (flexible) latch for quiet, corrosion-free, forgiving closure on coolers and lockers, and an adjustable or locking steel latch for higher loads or security (Boat Outfitters; Southco; RS).
guidance.when_not_to_use: Avoid it where the latch must be flush or hidden (use a concealed latch, quarter-turn fastener or magnetic catch), where the part is opened constantly with no need for pull-down force (a simple snap fit, magnetic catch or ball catch is enough), where real security is needed (add a padlock or use a cam lock), and where the latch sticks out and could be knocked open or catch on things. Don't use it as the only closure for something under internal pressure or that must never open in service without a secondary safety catch (US 4,925,221).
guidance.environment_limits: Zinc-plated steel and zinc die-castings corrode outdoors; stainless steel suits marine and washdown use (RS; Boat Outfitters). EPDM rubber latches resist corrosion and damp vibration, but rubber ages; the Firgelli blog claims UV and heat cycling can cost rubber latches 20-30% of their preload within three years [uncertain]. Printed latches: PLA softens above about 60 °C and PETG is fine below about 80 °C (Prusa), and PLA latches can creep and loosen over time (zx82net). The over-centre lock resists vibration, but a latch set only just past centre can shake open, so vibration-critical uses add a secondary safety catch (US 4,925,221).
guidance.safety_notes: Pinch point: fingers can be trapped between the lever and the base, or between the lid and the box, as it snaps shut [uncertain]. A tightly set lever can flick up when released, because the squeezed gasket and stretched loop push back [uncertain]. A latch that looks closed may be sitting on centre and unlocked if it is badly adjusted (US 4,925,221). Don't rely on a printed latch where failure could hurt someone.
guidance.common_failures: 1) Won't close, or needs two hands: the keeper is too far away or the gasket too thick; move or shim the keeper, or use an adjustable latch. 2) Closes loosely or rattles: the keeper is too close or has moved (loose screws), or the loop has stretched; re-set the keeper, tighten screws, use an adjustable hook. 3) Pops open under vibration or knocks: it is only just past centre, or on centre; adjust so it clearly snaps over, and add a secondary catch if needed (US 4,925,221). 4) Keeper or its screws pull out before the latch fails: rate and fix the keeper as strongly as the latch (RS). 5) Printed latches break at the layer lines or creep loose; improve layer adhesion, use PETG and metal pins (Glenn Brockett; zx82net). 6) Rubber latches crack or lose tension with age and sunlight; replace them periodically [uncertain].
related: Over-centre linkage (toggle linkage): the principle a draw latch is built on
Toggle clamp (latch-action type): a heavy-duty draw latch, usually with a threaded U-bolt, for doors and lids and for fixtures
Eccentric cam lever: a cam that is flipped past its high point instead of a linkage; also used on some case latches
Cam lock (quarter-turn latch): turns a cam behind the frame with a key or knob; flush and more secure, but draws the parts together less
Snap fit (cantilever clip): a springy printed clip; simpler and cheaper, but gives little or no pull-down force
Magnetic catch or ball catch: holds a door lightly closed with no lever and no clamping force
Hasp and staple: a hinged strap that goes over a staple for a padlock; secures but does not pull the parts together
Wire-bail closure (swing-top bottle, clip-top jar): the same over-centre pull-down made of bent wire, pressing a stopper or glass lid onto a rubber seal
